title: Sell Mineral Rights in Byron, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Byron, WY | Big Horn County
metaDescription: Byron, WY shares its name with one of Wyoming's oldest oil fields. Get a courthouse-checked, honest read on your Big Horn County mineral interest.
heroLead: Byron field takes its name from this town, and it's been producing oil since the early days of Bighorn Basin development, which makes Byron one of the few places on this list where the town and the geology share a name for a reason.
intro: The Byron field has been under production long enough to have gone through primary recovery, water injection, and further enhanced-recovery work over the decades, the kind of sustained development you only see in a field that's proven durable. Big Horn County recorder records for this area go back accordingly far, with leases, unit agreements, and probate filings stacked up across multiple generations of ownership.

If your family's interest sits inside the Byron field boundary, there's real production history to price against. If it sits just outside, on undeveloped acreage nearby, that's a different conversation, and I'll tell you honestly which situation applies before quoting anything.

sections.heading: A century of production in one place
paragraphs: Fields that stay productive this long typically do so because operators keep reinvesting in secondary and enhanced recovery once primary production tapers off. That ongoing investment is a signal there's still recoverable oil in place, which matters when I'm assessing whether your interest has meaningful runway left.
It also means the decline curve on a mature interest like this tends to be gentle year over year, unlike the steep early drop-off you'd see from a new horizontal well elsewhere in the state.

sections.heading: Untangling old family ownership
paragraphs: With this much history, it's common for a Byron-area mineral interest to have passed through several estates since the original lease was signed. I trace the Big Horn County recorder's grantor-grantee index back as far as needed to confirm your exact fractional share before we talk numbers.

I've also seen unit agreements from this field that predate modern legal formatting entirely, typed on old forms with hand-filled section numbers. They're still perfectly valid, and I know how to read them.

faqs.question: Is Byron field still producing today?
faqs.answer: Yes, portions continue under enhanced recovery methods. I'll check the current status tied specifically to your interest.

faqs.question: I have old royalty statements going back decades. Does that help?
faqs.answer: Significantly. A long documented production history gives me real numbers to price against rather than estimates.

faqs.question: What if my tract has never actually produced?
faqs.answer: Some acreage near Byron falls outside the field's actual productive boundary. I'll price that honestly as undeveloped acreage.

faqs.question: How far back can you trace ownership in this area?
faqs.answer: As far as the original homestead patent if needed. Big Horn County records go back to the early 1900s in most cases.
